title: Multidimensional dynamical centrality from Green functions in complex networks
abstract: Conventional centrality measures provide compact descriptions of node importance, but they emphasize specific structural relations and do not directly resolve the temporal and spectral organization of dynamical perturbation responses. Building on the Green function of a linearized networked system, we develop a multidimensional framework for dynamical node characterization. From the same response function, we extract three complementary indicators---Influence, Efficiency, and Distortion---that quantify cumulative response strength, temporal rate of response, and spectral concentration, respectively, together with a contribution matrix that resolves these quantities into source--target pathways. As a numerical demonstration, we apply the framework to weighted Kuramoto--Sakaguchi dynamics on heterogeneous Barabási--Albert networks. The three indicators distinguish implanted dynamical node classes through complementary dimensions of the perturbation response, while remaining strongly coupled to conventional topological centralities. These results demonstrate how a common dynamical response can be decomposed into distinct, physically interpretable characteristics rather than represented by a single aggregate descriptor. We finally discuss the scope and limitations of the linear-response assumption and extensions to time-dependent and nonlinear regimes.
summary: This paper introduces a novel, multidimensional method to characterize node importance in complex networks by analyzing the system's response to small perturbations via the Green function. It extracts three complementary metrics—Influence, Efficiency, and Distortion—which quantify different aspects of how a perturbation propagates. This approach moves beyond single structural measures by providing a detailed, physically interpretable decomposition of dynamical node behavior.
main_problem: Conventional centrality measures are insufficient because they only capture structural relations and fail to resolve the temporal and spectral organization of dynamical perturbation responses.
main_result: The framework successfully decomposes a common dynamical response into three distinct, physically interpretable characteristics: Influence, Efficiency, and Distortion.
method: The study develops a multidimensional characterization framework by analyzing the Green function of a linearized networked system.
model_or_system: The framework is applied to weighted Kuramoto–Sakaguchi dynamics on heterogeneous Barabási–Albert networks, modeling coupled oscillators on a complex network structure.
key_observables: Influence (cumulative response strength), Efficiency (temporal rate of response), and Distortion (spectral concentration), alongside a source--target contribution matrix.
important_parameters: The analysis is performed on BA networks with specific parameters (e.g., N=200, m=4) and involves time-window truncation for numerical stability.
main_assumptions: The analysis fundamentally relies on the linear-response assumption, which limits its applicability to strong perturbations or highly nonlinear regimes.
figures_summary: The notes mention a correlation analysis (Table I) comparing the three dynamical measures against conventional structural centralities (Degree, Betweenness, etc.).
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the need for a multidimensional characterization, then details the linear-response construction using the Green function, defines the three indicators (I, E, D) and their contribution matrix, and finally validates the approach numerically and discusses limitations.
why_interesting: The methodology of using linear response theory (Green functions) to extract multiple, complementary dynamical metrics (temporal, spectral, cumulative) is highly relevant to analyzing open quantum systems or complex many-body dynamics where single metrics fail to capture full system behavior.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Comparison between dynamical and topological cen- trality spaces. (a) Distribution of nodes in the dynamical centrality space defined by Influence I, Efficiency E, and Dis- tortion D. Normal nodes are colored according to their degree centrality, while superbroadcasters and slow nodes are high- lighted by red diamonds and blue squares, respectively. (b) Distribution of the same nodes in the conventional topological centrality space defined by degree, betweenness, and closeness centralities.
FIG. 2. Pearson correlation matrix among the three dynam- ical indicators and four topological centrality measures.

FIG. 3. Time-integrated contribution profiles of a superbroadcaster and a slow node. The bars show the fractional contribution Pis of each target node to the total Influence of the corresponding source node.

FIG. 4. Early-time contribution density Cis(t) for representative target nodes at one-, two-, and three-hop topological distances from the source. The source node itself is excluded. Curves are grouped by hop distance from the source.

FIG. 5. Robustness of the three dynamical indicators across 20 independent BA network realizations. Boxes span the interquar- tile range; horizontal lines mark the median. Whiskers extend to the most extreme values within 1.5 times the interquartile range.
